title: The Long Speech
tagline: A prime minister who had his speeches typed like poems, and how to carry a twenty-minute talk in nested palaces without losing your place.
card: Longer speeches: nested palaces, the rule of three, transition anchors and timing, plus the performance habits of a practised speaker.
goal: you will plan a longer speech as a main palace with a small room for each section, add anchors for transitions, and rehearse for timing and delivery.

left_off.q: Name the four tools for making an abstract idea concrete.
left_off.a: A symbol, a person, a scene and a feeling.

left_off.q: What did Aquinas advise to help memory?
left_off.a: Order, striking images, close attention and going over things often.

left_off.q: What should you do if a picture does not bring back the idea?

story.heading: A speech laid out like a poem

text: London, 1940. A prime minister is about to give a speech that the whole country is waiting to hear. He does not read it from a page of dense paragraphs. His secretaries have typed it in short lines, with extra space between phrases, in a layout they called psalm form because it looked like a psalm in a prayer book.

Winston Churchill, famous for his speeches, wrote them out in full and went over them again and again. But on the day he did not trust them to a block of text. The layout told his eye where to breathe, where to pause, and where the next idea began.

check.a: A way of typing a speech in short lines with spaces, so the speaker can see where to pause and where each idea starts.

parts.talk: How do you prepare when you must speak for a long time? Do you write it out?

text: There is a lesson in it for memory. A long speech is not one thing. It is a series of small pieces, each with its own beginning, middle and end. If you know where each piece starts, you can always find your way.

A twenty-minute talk is too long for a single list of five pictures. But it is easy for a speaker with a main palace, in which each room holds one section, and in which each section has its own small chain of pictures, like drawers in a cabinet.

check.q: How can a long speech be kept in mind?
check.a: As a series of small pieces: a main palace with one room per section, and a small chain of pictures in each.

parts.talk: Think of a speech or lecture you remember. Can you say what its sections were?

text: The best speakers also use patterns that listeners can follow without effort. The oldest is the rule of three: ideas in threes feel complete, and are easy to remember for both the speaker and the audience. Another is the return: an image or phrase that comes back at the end.

In this lesson you will plan a longer speech, add small anchors between the sections, and rehearse it aloud the way a performer does: for timing, for breath, and for the moment when everything goes wrong and you must carry on.

check.q: What is the rule of three?
check.a: Ideas in threes feel complete and are easy to remember.

parts.talk: Say three words, in order, that describe how you want your audience to feel at the end of a talk.

words.m: the move from one part of a talk to the next.
here: a fixed picture that marks a turning point in a speech.
choosing how long to spend on each part.
placed inside something larger of the same kind. A small palace nested inside a room.

source: The 'psalm form' layout of Churchill's speech notes is described by his secretaries. Retold here in our own words.
method_heading: Nested palaces for a longer talk

method.x: For a talk of about twenty minutes, use a main palace for the sections and a small chain in each room for the details.

items.h: Break the talk into five or six sections.
items.x: Opening, three main parts (the rule of three), a return, a close.
The main palace: door, hall, living room, kitchen, stairs, bedroom.

items.h: Put one big picture in each room.
items.x: This is the section's title: what the room is about.

items.h: Add a short chain of three or four details in the room.
items.x: On furniture or walls: statistics, examples, the story.

items.h: Add an anchor at every turn.
items.x: A fixed gesture or picture: a door opening at each new section.

method.title: A twenty-minute talk on a town's new library
lines: A giant book is knocking on the door and a crowd cheers: 'Welcome!'
A cracked old roof leaks rain on the books; three buckets in a row: leaks, cold, crowding.
Three armchairs: children, students, retired people, each reading a different glowing book.
Coins pouring from a pot, counted in three bowls: council, donors, volunteers.
The giant book from the door walks up the stairs, now wearing a crown.
A lamp is switched on over a pillow made of pages: 'Come back tomorrow'.
method.pic: One main palace, six rooms, and three little chains: the whole twenty minutes is a walk.

items: Time each section. Say the speech aloud with a clock. Mark where you are at the halfway point.
Practise the pauses. A pause before an important point lets the audience catch up.
Practise recovery. Stop in the middle on purpose, and find the next picture. You will be glad you did.
Use the body. Your ten body pegs (lesson 3) can hold the ten most important phrases, if you need them on stage.
Calm the start. Breathe out slowly, and look at the first place on your route.

method.x:
rooms for sections.
chains for details.
anchors for turns.
Say the six sections of the library talk aloud, in order, with one picture for each.

try.title: Plan a long talk
try.prompt: Choose a subject you could talk about for ten to twenty minutes. Write five or six sections, with one big picture for each.
try.model: Subject: why people should walk more. 1 Opening: giant shoes at the door. 2 Health: a heart jogging. 3 Money: a piggy bank on legs. 4 Mood: a smiling sun. 5 Return: the giant shoes again, now with wings. 6 Close: a path stretching into the horizon.
checks: A return to the opening picture.

try.title: Add details
try.prompt: Pick two sections. For each, write a chain of three details (facts or examples) as pictures on the furniture of the room.
try.model: Health room: on the sofa, a cushion shaped like a heart; on the table, a pill bottle dancing; on the window, a weighing scale with wings. Money room: on the fridge, coins; on the stove, a smiling wallet; on the shelf, a ticket to the cinema.
checks: Three details for each of two sections.
Each detail has its own place in the room.

try.title: Anchors
try.prompt: Write one fixed anchor you will use at every change of section (a gesture, a step, a picture of a door opening).
try.model: Every time I move to a new section I take one step forward and picture a door swinging open.
checks: The anchor is something I can do or see every time.

items.s: Ideas in groups of ___ feel complete and are easy to remember.
A fixed picture that marks a turning point is an ___.
A short stop in speaking is a ___.

try.q: A speaker loses their place in the middle of a section. What helps most?
opts: A fixed picture for the next section that they can walk to
try.why: A fixed route lets you jump to the next lesson and carry on.

try.title: Deliver it
try.prompt: Give the first three sections of your speech aloud, walking through your palace in your head, and use your anchor at each turn.

cards: One room for each section of the speech.
Three or four detail pictures on the furniture.
A fixed gesture or picture at each turn.
An image or phrase that comes back at the end.
Time it, practise pauses, practise recovery.

quiz.q: How many sections does a twenty-minute talk need?
quiz.why: Five or six sections, each with a few details.

challenge.intro: Learn the six sections of the library talk in order: opening, why it was needed, what it offers, what it cost, the return, the close.
